newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Zhu visit underpins closer Sino-Australian ties.
newsitem.headline: Zhu visit underpins closer Sino-Australian ties.

text.p: Chinese Vice-Premier Zhu Rongji left Australia on Friday after a week-long visit which underpinned a recent improvement in bilateral ties.
Among the trip's results were agreement on an unprecedented human rights dialogue later this year and a promise from China to boost iron ore investment and wool purchases.
"I truly believe that China and Australia are countries friendly to each other," said Zhu during the visit. "They have a bright future and very broad prospects for economic cooperation and trade."

The visit -- Zhu is the highest-ranking Chinese to visit Australia for three years -- was a payback for Australia's decision not to abandoning a United Nations' resolution censuring China over its human rights record.

There were small human rights protests against Zhu in Adelaide and Sydney, but nothing to cause embarrassment. Relations had cooled noticeably last year after a series of diplomatic and security spats.
"Australia and China can be described as partners building a peaceful, prosperous and cooperative Asia-Pacific region," said Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
The human rights dialogue, the communist nation's first such bilateral forum, is now scheduled to start in Beijing in August in the next step in the new relationship.
The two countries agreed in April to establish the formal dialogue with Australia saying the talks were the only way to achieve an improvement in China's human rights performance.
Downer and Zhu also played down concerns over regional security alliances, saying Australia's defence links, particularly with the United States, presented no problem.

The government-run China Daily newspaper had revived concerns during Zhu's visit in a long opinion piece saying an Australian security pact with the United States was part of China containment policy.
"There has existed traditional friendship between our two peoples and neither of us poses any threat to the other," Zhu said about the security pact.
China is Australia's fifth largest trading partner with two-way trade worth A$8.0 billion (US$6.1 billion) in 1996.
Trade is growing about 20 percent a year and China is expected to become Australia's number two trade partner by 2005.
